title: Spaghetti ai Ricci di Mare
subtitle: spaghetti with fresh sea urchin roe
excerpt: Spaghetti ai ricci di mare is a Puglian and Sicilian pasta dressed with fresh sea urchin roe, olive oil, garlic, chilli, and parsley. The roe is not cooked; it melts into the oiled pasta off the heat. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Spaghetti ai ricci di mare (pasta with sea urchin roe) is a speciality of the Adriatic and Ionian coasts of southern Italy, particularly Puglia and the Salento peninsula, where ricci di mare (sea urchins, principally Paracentrotus lividus) are gathered from rocky shores. The dish also appears along the Sicilian north and west coasts. The preparation is similar to bottarga pasta in principle: a raw seafood product of intense flavour is applied to hot oiled pasta off the heat. Direct cooking of sea urchin roe is generally avoided as it renders the roe grainy and loses the clean, briny, sweet flavour. The dish is documented in Jeanne Caròla Francesconi, La cucina napoletana (1965, Fausto Fiorentino Editore), and in regional Puglian cooking guides.

glossaryTerms.term: Ricci di mare / sea urchin roe
glossaryTerms.definition: The golden-orange gonads (roe) of sea urchins, sold cleaned and ready to eat in small trays. The flavour is intensely savoury, sweet, and oceanic. They dissolve into oiled pasta when tossed, coating each strand with a rich, briny flavour. Do not apply direct heat.

content.text: di mare is the most extravagant of the simple southern Italian pasta dishes. The sea urchin roe, orange and soft, goes directly onto the oiled pasta off the heat. It melts into the oil and pasta water to coat each strand in a flavour that is simultaneously sweet, briny, and deeply savoury. No cooking, no sauce-building: just quality roe, quality oil, and the technique of keeping the pan away from the flame.

Fresh roe from a fishmonger is the correct ingredient; it is sometimes labelled ricci or sea urchin roe and sold in small trays. Ready-to-use sea urchin roe in jars (pasteurised) is also available online; it works but the flavour is less vivid. Do not use synthetic sea urchin paste. The dish is nothing without the real thing.

items.prepNote: fresh or pasteurised, from a fishmonger
taste before adding; roe may be salty

content.text: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Cook {{pasta-dried}} of spaghetti until al dente. Reserve 150 ml of pasta cooking water.

While the pasta cooks, warm {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large saute pan over a low heat. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and chilli flakes. Cook for 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant but not coloured. Add the white wine if using and let it bubble for 30 seconds. Remove from the heat.

Drain the pasta and add to the pan off the heat. Toss to coat in the garlic oil. Add {{sea-urchin-roe}} of sea urchin roe, {{lemon-juice}} of lemon juice, and {{parsley-flat}} of parsley. Toss gently with a splash of pasta water: the roe will begin to dissolve into the oil and water, coating the pasta. Do not return the pan to the heat.
Taste for salt (the roe may be sufficient). Serve immediately in warm bowls. No cheese.

items.symptom: Roe turns grainy and loses its creamy texture
items.cause: Pan was still over heat when roe was added
items.fix: Always add sea urchin roe completely off the heat. The residual warmth of the pasta is sufficient to melt it into the oil.

items.cause: Roe not fresh, or too little used
items.fix: Sea urchin roe should be used the day it is bought. The flavour fades quickly. 100 g for 4 is a minimum; more is better.

content.text: Ricci di mare pasta is from the rocky coastlines of the Salento (the heel of Italy's boot), Puglia, and parts of Sicily where sea urchins are gathered by hand from the rocks at low tide. In Taranto, Gallipoli, and Otranto, the dish is a fixture of summer restaurant menus. In winter, the roe is richer and more flavourful, which makes December to February the best season despite the cold. Outside Italy, sea urchin roe is available from Japanese fishmongers (where it is called uni) and from specialist Italian delis. The dish has no substitutes and no shortcuts; it is worth making only when the roe is very good.
